To describe what life was like “in the old days”.
An autumn Sunday. Ana and Mihai are at Grandma Rosario’s. Ana has found a box of old records and letters in the wardrobe. Grandma smiles mysteriously.
Grandma, whose letters are these? They’re signed by someone called “A.”.
Oh, darling… They’re from your grandfather, Andrés. From when we were courting, in 1964.
And why did you write each other letters if you lived in the same village?
Because my father didn’t want us to see each other. He was very strict. He wanted me to marry the chemist’s son.
Really? And what did you do?
At first, nothing. In those days it was normal for parents to decide those things. And girls weren’t allowed to go out alone.
So how did you meet Grandpa?
At the San Juan fiesta. My mother let me go, but she asked me to be back before ten.
And were you back at ten?
At half past twelve. Andrés asked me to dance one song with him… and we danced twenty.
He forbade me to leave the house for a month. That’s why we wrote to each other. My little sister carried the letters in her apron pocket.
How romantic… And how did you win him over in the end?
I didn’t. Your grandfather did. He came to the house and asked my father to listen to him for five minutes. He talked for an hour.
And what did he say to him?
I never found out. But when he came out, my father told me to put on my nice dress, because the three of us were going to Mass.
The nice dress… the same one I wore at my wedding?
The very same, darling. That’s why I wanted you to wear it.

Both forms are correct and mean the same. In speech you hear -ra more often: FWEH-ra. The -se form (FWEH-seh) appears mostly in writing and in northern Spain.
ber-BEH-na: both “b” and “v” are pronounced the same. It’s the summer fiesta with music and dancing in Madrid’s neighbourhoods.
1. The imperfect subjunctive: from the indefinido
This is one of the most regular forms in Spanish, if you know the indefinido (chapter 15). Take the “ellos” form of the indefinido, drop -ron and add the -ra endings:
Excellent news: ALL the irregularities of the indefinido carry over automatically. If you know “tuvieron”, you know “tuviera”. Nothing new to memorise!
There’s also a second form, in -se, which is exactly equivalent: hablase, tuviese, fuese. You’ll meet it in books. You can always use the -ra form.
“fuera” is the subjunctive of both SER and IR. Context decides: Quería que fuera feliz (that she be happy) / Quería que fuera al baile (that she go to the dance).

The rule: if the main verb (the one that triggers the subjunctive) is in the PRESENT, use the PRESENT subjunctive. If it’s in the PAST (imperfect, indefinido, conditional), use the IMPERFECT subjunctive.
In English, “to come” doesn’t change: “I want you TO COME” / “I wanted you TO COME”. In Spanish it does: quería que VINIERAS. Listen for the “echo” of the tense: past in front → past after que.
4. Verbs of influence: pedir, prohibir, permitir
Verbs by which someone tries to influence what another person does take the subjunctive:
Me pidió que volviera antes de las diez.
Mi padre me prohibió que saliera.
Mi madre me permitió que fuera.
decir que (= to tell someone to)
Me dijo que me pusiera el vestido.
Le aconsejé que no se preocupara.
Careful with “decir”! If it passes on INFORMATION → indicative: Me dijo que estaba cansado. If it passes on an ORDER / REQUEST → subjunctive: Me dijo que me pusiera el vestido.
With permitir, prohibir and dejar you can also use the infinitive: Me prohibió salir = Me prohibió que saliera.
5. How to talk about “the old days”
For memories and “how things used to be”, combine the imperfect (setting, habits) with the imperfect subjunctive (what was expected, what was normal):
In those days it was normal for girls not to go out alone.
My parents wanted me to study medicine, but I wanted to be a painter.
Nobody expected us to get married so young.
Useful phrases: en aquella época, en aquellos tiempos, cuando yo era joven, antes (before, in the past), de joven.
My parents wanted me to study medicine.
My mother let me go to the dance.

Hablar con el padre de Rosario
Lo que dijo el abuelo Andrés
That afternoon, Ana couldn’t stop thinking about one question: what had Grandpa Andrés said to Rosario’s father during that hour?
Grandma didn’t know. Grandpa had died twelve years earlier. And her great-grandfather, the strict father, forty years before that.
But there was someone who might know: Great-aunt Lola, the little sister who carried the letters in her apron. She was eighty-four and lived in a care home in Toledo.
The following Saturday, Ana and Mihai went to Toledo. Aunt Lola was waiting for them in the garden, sitting in the sun, with a straw hat and enormous glasses.
“Anita! How pretty you are. And this is the Romanian, isn’t it? Rosario told me you dance terribly.”
Mihai went red. Ana laughed and sat down next to her.
“Auntie, we wanted to ask you something. Do you know what Grandpa Andrés said to your father that day?”
Aunt Lola slowly took off her glasses. For a moment she looked out at the yellow fields around the city.
“Of course I know. I was hiding behind the kitchen door. I was twelve and very nosy.”
Ana and Mihai looked at each other. Fifty years of mystery were about to end.
“My father was a very hard man,” Aunt Lola began. “He had lost two brothers in the war and he was afraid of everything. Above all, he was afraid his daughters would suffer.”
“He wanted Rosario to marry the chemist’s son because he was rich. Not because she loved him. He thought money would protect her.”
“Andrés had no money. He was the baker’s son. He worked from four in the morning.”
“That day, Andrés came into the house with his hands covered in flour. He hadn’t changed his clothes. My father asked him to sit down, very seriously.”
“Andrés didn’t talk about love. That’s what surprised me most. I expected him to say romantic things, like in the films. But no.”
“He talked to my father about bread.”
“About bread. He told him he got up at four every day so the village would have warm bread. That he had never missed a single day. Not when he was ill, not when his mother died.”
“He told him: ‘Sir, I can’t promise you your daughter will be rich. But I promise she will never go without bread. Neither the bread on the table nor the other kind.’”
“That’s exactly what my father asked him. And Andrés answered: ‘Our daily bread, sir. Being there. Someone waiting up for her when she comes home late. Someone remembering how she likes her coffee.’”
Aunt Lola fell silent. A light breeze stirred the leaves of the trees.
“My father didn’t say anything for a long time. Then he stood up and went into the kitchen, and I had to run so he wouldn’t see me.”
“He came back with two glasses of wine. He gave one to Andrés and said: ‘Tomorrow, Mass. All three of us.’ Nothing more.”
Ana had tears in her eyes. Mihai took her hand.
“Andrés asked me not to tell her. He said promises aren’t to be told: they’re to be kept. And he kept his. Fifty years of warm bread and coffee just the way she liked it.”
“But he’s gone now,” said Aunt Lola, looking at Ana. “So I think you can tell her now. I’m sure Andrés wouldn’t mind.”
That evening, in the car on the way back to Madrid, Mihai was very quiet.
“What are you thinking about?” Ana asked him.
“That I don’t know how to make bread,” he answered. “But I know how you like your coffee. With lots of milk and half a teaspoon of sugar. And lukewarm, never too hot.”
Ana smiled and looked out of the window. The lights of Madrid were appearing on the horizon.
The next day, Ana went to see Grandma Rosario. Under her arm she had a warm loaf of bread. And a story that had waited fifty years to be told.
